tldr: World-Coherent-Decoding (WCD) identifies good and bad future predictions generated by World Action Models (WAMs) using pre-execution internal generative signals. It then self-verifies them against realized observations after execution, substantially improving robot manipulation success without retraining the backbone model.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method, WCD. Before execution (Phase 1), internal signals select the best candidate. After execution (Phase 2), the prediction is compared against realized observations to compute self-verification error. A lightweight predictor is trained online on this accumulated data to guide future candidate selection (Phase 3).
overview:
In robot control, World Action Models (WAMs) are attracting widespread attention as an alternative to Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that output actions directly from observations. WAMs first imagine visual future changes as video rollouts and then decode actions. While embedding physical intuition via video prediction is an appealing approach, it comes with a major catch: the stochasticity of video generation. Even starting from the exact same situation, models sometimes hallucinate non-existent objects or imagine physically impossible motions, causing action decoding to fail.

To address this, the authors focus on a structural strength inherent to WAMs: the falsifiability of future predictions. Once the robot takes an action, the real world checks whether that imagination was correct. The challenge is a temporal gap: at the moment of deciding an action, the future reality is not yet observable. To bridge this gap, the authors propose World-Coherent-Decoding (WCD). Before execution, WCD estimates plausibility using internal generative traces (video flow surprisal and action path effort). After execution, it uses the mismatch with reality to train a lightweight online predictor.

Experiments on the bimanual benchmark RoboTwin 2.0 and a real Franka arm demonstrate that early imagination-reality mismatch directly correlates with task failure rates. Particularly under challenging conditions with unseen environmental changes, WCD improves average success on Hard tasks from $55.80\%$ to $60.90\%$ without any fine-tuning of the backbone model, achieving a substantial $+16.43$ point gain on long-horizon tasks. This work clearly shows that test-time scaling depends less on merely sampling more futures than on selecting reliable ones.
contributions: Formulated robot control with World Action Models (WAMs) as a reliability-based candidate selection problem, highlighting the structural property that pre-execution imaginations are falsifiable by post-execution reality.
Proposed WCD, which ranks candidates using only internal signals—flow-based video surprisal and action path effort—without any external verifiers or task rewards.

Constructed an online learning mechanism for a lightweight predictor trained on the delayed self-verification signal (mismatch with realized observations), amortizing the high computational cost of internal signals into fast pre-execution estimates.
Demonstrated the effectiveness of test-time scaling by substantially improving success rates on the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark and real Franka visual-shift tests while keeping the backbone model frozen.

sections.heading: How to Spot a Robot's Hallucination? Exploiting the Falsifiability of Imagination
sections.summary: WAMs are a powerful framework that predicts future video before deriving actions, but they risk failure due to generative variance. The authors discovered substantial reliability differences among predictions sampled from the same condition, motivating a new test-time planning framework self-verified by realized observations after execution.
sections.details:
Recently, World Action Models (WAMs) that predict physical dynamics as video rollouts have emerged as alternatives to Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which directly output joint commands from images and text. Predicting video before solving for actions is essentially setting an implicit goal and then solving inverse dynamics. This brings a major advantage: robustness against environmental shifts.

However, video generation is inherently stochastic. Given the same observation history and text prompt, the model sometimes generates a plausible future, but other times hallucinates non-existent obstacles or warped gripper positions.

### Pilot Study: Imagination Reliability Has Selectable Variance
The authors first conducted a pilot study sampling multiple future predictions from a fixed observation history and comparing them to the realized video rollout obtained afterward. They found a wide spread in error relative to reality (latent-space mismatch), even among predictions generated from the same prompt. Furthermore, rollouts with larger mismatches in initial steps showed dramatically higher final task failure rates.

This led to a core insight: WAM imaginations are falsifiable. Once an action is executed, the real world automatically grades the prediction. No external reward function or success classifier is needed. However, the action must be selected before execution. To bridge this temporal gap, the authors propose World-Coherent-Decoding (WCD), combining pre-execution internal signals with post-execution feedback.

captions.F1: Results of the pilot study. (a) Even when sampled from the same observation history, post-hoc errors vary widely (green is best, brown is worst). (b) This variance is universal across diverse tasks. (c) Core concept of WCD, combining pre-execution internal scores with post-execution self-verification feedback.

sections.heading: Generative Candidate Selection and Test-Time Planning for Robotics
sections.summary: This section reviews prior works leveraging test-time computation, such as Best-of-N sampling in text-to-image generation and value function guidance in robotics. This study stands out by remaining entirely self-contained within the world model's internal signals without using additional pretrained evaluators or reward labels.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of two major research directions.

### Sampling and Selection in Stochastic Generative Models
In image generation, Best-of-$N$ sampling—selecting the best image using reward models or human preferences—and test-time noise optimization are widely used. This paper extends this selection concept to robot control. For robots, however, the target of selection is not a single static image, but a future video and action-chunk pair, which must be evaluated before physical feedback arrives.

### Test-Time Guidance for Robot Policies
Recent research on robot foundation models has also explored increasing test-time compute to boost performance, such as value-guided sampling or external verifier-based action filtering. However, these methods depend on additional reward annotations or pretrained evaluation networks. The key strength of this approach is that it requires zero extra supervision: it relies solely on internal generative signals from the world model itself and the physical observations obtained naturally after execution.

sections.heading: How WCD Works: Internal Signal Filtering and Delayed Self-Verification
sections.summary: WCD samples $N$ future-action candidates from a frozen WAM, ranking them by video surprisal and action smoothness. After execution, the mismatch with reality serves as supervision to train a lightweight predictor online, enabling faster and more accurate candidate selection.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Preliminaries: Chunked World Models and Falsifiability
Given a cache of past observations and actions $C_m$, the base WAM uses Flow Matching to generate a future latent video $\hat{z}$, and then decodes low-level action chunks $a$. Once the action is executed, the real latent observation $z^{\mathrm{real}}$ becomes available, enabling a post-hoc reality check.

### 3.2 Pre-Execution Candidate Selection via Internal Generative Signals
At decision step $m$, $N$ candidates are sampled while keeping the model frozen. These candidates are evaluated using two internal signals:
- **Video Flow Surprisal**: Computes the divergence of the velocity field during video generation using the Hutchinson trace estimator. Traversing regions with positive divergence lowers the probability density, meaning the model is imagining a wilder, high-surprisal future. Lower surprisal indicates visual changes that closely follow the training distribution.
- **Action Path Effort**: Accumulates step-by-step updates $\Delta a$ across the action denoising trajectory. A smaller value indicates decisive, smooth, and stable action generation.

These two scores are min-max normalized and combined to select and execute the highest-scoring candidate.

### 3.3 Delayed Self-Verification (Backward Error)
After execution, the squared error between the imagined latent $\hat{z}$ and the realized latent $z^{\mathrm{real}}$ (backward error $b_m$) is computed. If this error exceeds the historical running mean, the visual prediction is deemed unreliable in the current context, automatically reducing the video score weight $\lambda_m$.

### 3.4 Online Calibration: Amortizing Delayed Error into a Predictor
While flow surprisal is principled, its gradient computation incurs high computational cost. To mitigate this, a small regression model $f_\psi$ is introduced to predict the post-execution backward error directly from lightweight sampling-time features (such as denoising velocity norms and inter-frame differences in latent space).
Initially, candidates are chosen reliably using flow surprisal (Pre-warm). Once sufficient execution data accumulates in the replay buffer, the framework switches automatically to fast scoring via the trained predictor (Post-warm).

captions.F2: Two internal signals used for candidate selection. (a)-(c) On the video side, flow divergence is integrated to measure the drop in probability density (surprisal), identifying plausible rollouts. (d) On the action side, denoising path effort is computed to reward decisive and stable actions.
captions.F3: Overall architecture of WCD. In Phase 1, candidates are filtered using internal signals and executed. In Phase 2, the mismatch with reality is stored in a buffer. In Phase 3, a lightweight predictor is trained online and used for candidate selection in subsequent steps.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Robustness from Selection and the True Value of Test-Time Scaling
sections.summary: WCD was evaluated on the bimanual benchmark RoboTwin 2.0 and a real Franka arm. Early imagination error strongly correlates with task failure. Under limited randomization, WCD substantially boosts success rates, demonstrating that scaling candidate counts only works when paired with effective selection signals.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on RoboTwin 2.0 (50 tasks), covering diverse bimanual manipulation skills. In addition to the standard protocol where model performance is saturated, the authors designed a practically crucial "Limited-randomization" protocol. Models are pretrained on clean environments and fine-tuned on a small fraction of randomized data. While the model understands physical structures, its prediction quality fluctuates under test-time disturbances. Furthermore, a real Franka hammering task was tested under unseen visual shifts, such as colored lighting and camera defocus.

### 4.2 Main Results
- **Correlation Between Initial Error and Task Failure**: Measuring the mismatch between imagination and reality (backward error) across the first 3 chunks revealed that the lowest-error quartile had a failure rate of only $4.9\%$, whereas the highest-error quartile degraded to $21.2\%$. This confirms that self-verification signals strongly reflect task outcomes.
- **Gains in Limited-Randomization Settings**: Under the Limited-randomization Hard setting with substantial headroom, WCD improved the base model's success rate from $55.80\%$ to $60.90\%$ ($+5.10$ points) with a frozen backbone. On long-horizon Horizon-3 tasks requiring extended reasoning, it achieved a dramatic $+16.43$ point boost.
- **Robustness Under Real-World Stress**: Under real colored-lighting tests where baseline WAM and $\pi 0.5$ failed, WCD selected trajectories that accurately struck the target object and completed the task.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies
- **Component Contributions**: Random candidate selection ("Random-$N$") achieved only $53.5\%$ on Hard tasks. Surprisal, path effort, and the online predictor each provided independent gains, but combining all components reached the top performance of $60.90\%$.
- **Scaling Candidate Count $N$**: While naive sampling (Random-$N$) plateaus as candidate counts increase, WCD's selection signals enable steady performance improvements as $N$ scales up.

captions.F5: Relationship between early rollout imagination-reality mismatch (first 3 chunks) and task failure rate. As initial error quartiles increase, failure rates rise monotonically from $4.9\%$ to $21.2\%$, showing that self-verification error closely mirrors policy success.
captions.F6: Analysis of test-time scaling. (a) Simply increasing candidate count $N$ (Random-N) yields no gain, whereas pairing with selection signals improves success rates. (b) Performance gains are most pronounced on harder tasks with larger remaining headroom.
captions.F4: Evaluation setup for the real Franka hammering task. Models were trained in (a) normal conditions and evaluated under severe visual shifts unseen during training: (b) colored lighting, (c) lens defocus blur, and (d) cluttered distractor layouts.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: Smarter Test-Time Computation
sections.summary: WCD reframes world action model predictions as falsifiable hypotheses, presenting a new test-time planning framework that selects reliable actions without rewards or extra annotations. Future work includes reducing candidate generation overhead and optimizing for high-frequency control.
sections.details:
This work addressed generative variance in World Action Models (WAMs) by introducing WCD, a framework combining internal model signals with delayed self-verification. By selecting reliable future-action pairs at inference time without modifying the backbone weights, WCD demonstrated notable robustness gains across both simulation and real-world experiments.

Takeaway is clear: the essence of test-time scaling for WAMs lies not in blindly imagining more futures, but in reliably identifying which ones to trust.

Nevertheless, the computational overhead of sampling $N$ candidates remains a trade-off. While the online predictor significantly trims scoring overhead, speeding up base WAM generation and optimizing pipelines for high-frequency real-time control remain vital directions for future research.

takeaways: Future predictions from World Action Models are falsifiable hypotheses; mismatches with post-execution observations can be directly used as self-supervised signals.
Test-time Best-of-N sampling does not scale by volume alone; it requires effective selection signals like flow surprisal and action smoothness to unlock performance gains.
Using computationally heavy signals (Flow Surprisal) for a cold start and amortizing them into a lightweight online predictor trained on accumulated data is a highly practical design.
limitations: Generating and evaluating multiple future candidates increases parallel compute requirements and inference latency, requiring optimization before deployment in millisecond-level high-frequency control.
In clean environments where the base model's success rate is already saturated, candidate selection headroom is small, yielding limited performance improvements.
While the online predictor is shared across episodes, further investigation is needed regarding adaptation speed and resistance to catastrophic forgetting when task domains undergo radical shifts.
